title: Johansen/Weiss/Motzki, Islamic Law (Oxford Encyclopedia of Legal History)

slides.title: What the fiqh is, and what it is not
slides.text: The entry has six subentries — an overview, the sources and methodology, the genres of legal literature, the legal and ethical qualifications, the spheres of the law, and the transmission of the reports from the Prophet. Start with the term. The FIQH is a SYSTEM OF ETHICAL AND LEGAL NORMS, as a discipline with its own literature and methods dating FROM THE SECOND HALF OF THE EIGHTH CENTURY, and for the next 1,100 YEARS it embodied the discipline of legal thought in Islam. Before the ninth century the word fiqh — usually rendered 'jurisprudence' — meant no more than 'THE INDEPENDENT COMPREHENSION OF CONTEXTS AND INTERRELATIONS' or 'INSIGHT'. Its rules regulate ACTS OF WORSHIP (ʿIBĀDĀT) and TRANSACTIONS (MUʿĀMALĀT) between human beings, and — the decisive sentence of the whole article — they are WRITTEN DOWN OR TAUGHT ORALLY BY INDIVIDUAL RELIGIOUS SCHOLARS, NOT BY POLITICAL LAWGIVERS. From the eighth to the nineteenth century the fiqh REMAINS A JURISTS' LAW, produced, discussed and developed by scholars. Rules of worship are not normally under the control of the judiciary; rules governing transactions — marriage and family, commercial exchange, penal sanctions — are.

terms.def: The Islamic discipline of legal and ethical norms, from the 8th to the 19th century a JURISTS' law — made by scholars, not by political lawgivers.
The two great fields of the fiqh: acts of worship owed to God, and transactions between human beings — the second controlled by the judiciary, the first largely not.

cards.q: What is the fiqh, and what is the single most important thing about how its norms are made?
cards.a: A system of ethical and legal norms, a discipline with its own literature and methods from the second half of the EIGHTH century, governing acts of worship (ʿibādāt) and transactions (muʿāmalāt). Decisively, its rules are written down or taught by INDIVIDUAL RELIGIOUS SCHOLARS, NOT BY POLITICAL LAWGIVERS: from the 8th to the 19th century it remains a JURISTS' LAW.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: The jurists close the ranks
slides.text: The FUQAHĀʾ hold that their conduct-related rules constitute A NORMATIVE FIELD OF ITS OWN WITH METHODS, PROCEDURES AND TECHNICAL REASONING SO COMPLEX THAT ONLY SCHOLARS INSTRUCTED IN THEM CAN MASTER THEM. The consequence is institutional: the jurists EXCLUDE FROM THE CONSENSUS OF THE LEARNED (IJMĀʿ) — itself one of the sources of the law — THOSE MEMBERS OF THE RELIGIOUS DISCIPLINES WHO ARE NOT TRAINED AS JURISTS, AND THIS HOLDS TRUE EVEN FOR THE THEOLOGIANS, justified by their INCOMPETENCY IN THE FIELD OF LEGAL REASONING. This is a claim to professional autonomy made through the doctrine of sources: by defining who counts in the consensus, the jurists define who makes law.

terms.def: The consensus of the learned, one of the four sources of the law — from which the jurists excluded even theologians, on the ground of their incompetence in legal reasoning.

cards.q: How did the fiqh scholars secure their professional autonomy?
cards.a: By holding that their reasoning was so complex that only trained jurists could master it, and therefore EXCLUDING non-jurists — theologians included — from the CONSENSUS OF THE LEARNED (ijmāʿ), which is itself a source of the law. Defining who counts in the consensus is defining who makes law.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: The judiciary as the engine of the schools
slides.text: The fiqh quickly acquired the leading position in religious knowledge — the MADRASAS of the eleventh century were devoted primarily to the study of Islamic law, other disciplines assigned an AUXILIARY role. But the article insists on the role of the EMPIREWIDE JUDICIARY established by the ABBASID DYNASTY (750–1258) in the second half of the eighth century, with an administration under a CHIEF JUSTICE responsible for appointing and removing the QADIS in the provinces. The logic: AN EMPIREWIDE JUDICIARY REQUIRED NORMS WITH A CLAIM TO UNIVERSAL VALIDITY, and the burgeoning schools found in the administration of the judiciary AN IMPORTANT TOOL FOR SPREADING THEIR NORMS. Since the qadis mattered in the distribution and control of power in the cities, URBAN ELITES BECAME INTERESTED IN CONTROLLING THE OFFICE, and their competition ENCOURAGED IDENTIFICATION WITH SCHOOLS OF LAW as locally relevant instances of legitimisation. Doctrine spread because appointments did.

cards.q: What did the Abbasid judiciary do for the schools of law?
cards.a: The empirewide judiciary founded in the later 8th century, under a chief justice appointing and removing the qadis, required norms claiming UNIVERSAL validity — so the schools found in it the tool for spreading their doctrines. Urban elites competed for the office of qadi, and that competition made them identify with schools of law as instruments of local legitimisation. Doctrine spread because appointments did.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Dissent as a structural principle
slides.text: As a jurists' law the fiqh is INDIVIDUALISTIC in the production of norms, in DISSENT among jurists, and in the stress on the SUBJECTIVE RIGHTS OF THE INDIVIDUAL — which is why it produced a great number of SCHOOLS OF LAW. And the differences are not trivial: on who may become a PROTECTED SUBJECT of Muslim authority, the HANAFIS admitted everybody except Arab polytheists, even 'idolators and fire adorers'; the MALIKIS did not even exclude Arab polytheists; the HANBALIS AND SHAFIʿIS admitted ONLY MONOTHEISTS BELIEVING IN A SACRED BOOK, all others being left the choice AMONG CONVERSION, MIGRATION AND DEATH. Differences of that magnitude were accepted. From the tenth century a specialised genre treated DISSENT (KHILĀF) AS A HISTORICAL SUBJECT showing the magnitude of LICIT differences, and the legal literature acquired a HIGHLY DEVELOPED ARGUMENTATIVE STRUCTURE exposing dissent and the arguments for each choice. As Joseph Schacht put it, Islamic law is 'an objective law which guarantees the subjective rights of individuals… the sum total of the personal privileges of all individuals'.

terms.def: Dissent among jurists — from the 10th century a literary genre of its own, treating licit disagreement as a historical subject.

cards.q: How far did the disagreement between Islamic schools of law reach? Give the example.
cards.a: Far beyond secondary questions. On who could become a protected subject of Muslim authority: the Hanafis admitted all but Arab polytheists — even 'idolators and fire adorers'; the Malikis did not exclude even those; the Hanbalis and Shafiʿis admitted ONLY monotheists with a sacred book, leaving all others the choice among conversion, migration and death. Such differences were nonetheless accepted as licit.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What is khilāf, and why does the fiqh literature argue rather than state?
cards.a: Khilāf is dissent among jurists, from the tenth century a literary genre treating disagreement as a historical subject showing the magnitude of LICIT difference. Because dissent is a structural principle of a jurists' law, the literature developed a highly argumentative form — exposing the differences and the reasons that justify each choice, rather than simply announcing a rule.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Shariʿa and fiqh — the distinction everything turns on
slides.text: In the eighth and ninth centuries method and material were not separated. The separation begins with the question WHETHER LEGAL RULES MAY REST ON THE REASONED OPINION AND JURISTIC PREFERENCE OF THE JURISTS OR MUST REST ON THE QURʾAN AND THE SUNNA OR ANALOGIES FROM THEM — and the first book systematically distinguishing legal METHOD from legal MATERIAL is SHAFIʿI'S EPISTLE (RISĀLA), whose final version was written in Egypt BETWEEN 815 AND 820. The genre USUL AL-FIQH itself comes into existence only in the SECOND HALF OF THE TENTH CENTURY, more than a hundred years after Shafiʿi's death. And the payoff: because the fiqh became known as 'THE BRANCHES' whose 'ROOTS' were treated in another discipline, the discipline has HAD THE IMPORTANT MERIT OF CONSTANTLY REMINDING MUSLIMS THAT THE FIQH IS NOT IDENTICAL WITH ITS REVEALED SOURCE, THE SHARIʿA. IT IS A HISTORICAL FORM OF ITS INTERPRETATION. Hold on to that sentence — the modern half of the article depends on it entirely.

terms.def: The 'roots' of the fiqh: the theory of the sources of law and of legal argumentation, a genre from the second half of the 10th century. Prepared by Shafiʿi's Risāla (815–820).
The shariʿa is the revealed law; the fiqh is a HISTORICAL FORM OF ITS INTERPRETATION — the distinction that allows fiqh rules to be replaced without abandoning the shariʿa.

cards.q: State the distinction between shariʿa and fiqh, and say what the discipline of uṣūl al-fiqh achieved by it.
cards.a: The shariʿa is the revealed law; the FIQH IS NOT IDENTICAL WITH IT BUT A HISTORICAL FORM OF ITS INTERPRETATION. By treating the 'roots' in a separate discipline — leaving the fiqh as 'the branches' — uṣūl al-fiqh kept reminding Muslims of exactly that, which is the premise of every modern reform argument.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What is Shafiʿi's Risāla, and what is it NOT?
cards.a: The first book systematically distinguishing legal METHOD from legal MATERIAL, its final version written in Egypt between 815 and 820. It is NOT the first work of the genre uṣūl al-fiqh, though often called so: that genre arises only in the second half of the tenth century, over a hundred years after Shafiʿi's death, and with a different, theological approach.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Modern developments: codes, constitutions, and the shariʿa clauses
slides.text: From the END OF THE NINETEENTH CENTURY CODES WERE IMPORTED FROM THE WEST and replaced historical fiqh rules on transactions by modern CIVIL, PENAL AND COMMERCIAL CODES and codes of procedure; WRITTEN CONSTITUTIONS INTRODUCED THE POLITICAL LAWGIVER AS THE LEGISLATIVE POWER AND LEFT NO PLACE FOR A JURISTS' LAW. Under those circumstances the distinction between fiqh and shariʿa allowed the replacement of fiqh rules to be understood NOT AS A DESTRUCTION OF THE SHARIʿA BUT AS AN INVITATION TO DERIVE A NEW INTERPRETATION from the revealed sources. SINCE THE 1970s a great number of constitutions have made 'THE PRINCIPLES OF THE SHARIʿA' a or the principal source of legislation — Kuwait 1962, Egypt 1971 (amended 1980), the UAE 1971, Qatar 1972 and 2003, Bahrain 1973, Syria 1973, Yemen 1991, Mauritania 1991, Oman 1996, Sudan 1998; Pakistan's Objectives Resolution as Art. 2-A (1985), and Afghanistan's repugnancy clause in Art. 3 of the 2004 constitution: 'IN AFGHANISTAN, NO LAW CAN BE CONTRARY TO THE BELIEFS AND PROVISIONS OF THE SACRED RELIGION OF ISLAM'. And the point to notice: NONE of these constitutions refers to the RULES OF THE FIQH, and most do not even declare Qurʾanic verses self-enacting — they refer to PRINCIPLES (MABĀDIʾ AL-SHARIʿA), that is, TO SOMETHING THAT MUST BE DETERMINED BY LEGAL INTERPRETATION. In practice the fiqh in its classical form dominates national law in VERY FEW states.

terms.def: A constitutional provision making 'the principles of the shariʿa' a principal source of legislation — principles requiring interpretation, not the rules of the classical fiqh.

cards.q: What do the modern constitutional 'shariʿa clauses' actually refer to?
cards.a: To the PRINCIPLES of the shariʿa (mabādiʾ al-shariʿa) — something that must be DETERMINED BY LEGAL INTERPRETATION. None of these constitutions makes the RULES OF THE FIQH a principal source, and most do not even treat Qurʾanic verses as self-enacting. Courts and legislators reach the content through uṣūl al-fiqh or the 'aims of the shariʿa'.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: Why did the imported Western codes leave no place for a jurists' law?
cards.a: Because written constitutions introduced the POLITICAL LAWGIVER as the legislative power, and the codes of civil, penal and commercial law replaced the fiqh rules on transactions. A law produced by scholars has no room in a system where an elected legislator makes law — which is the structural break of the nineteenth century.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Weiss: what the shariʿa is, and who the source is
slides.text: In Muslim legal thought ALL LAW WORTHY OF THE NAME IS SUBSUMED UNDER THE MORE GENERAL CATEGORY OF SHARIʿA: a normative system embracing NOT ONLY STATE LAW BUT ALSO ETHICAL NORMS AND RITUAL DUTIES AND PROPRIETIES, carrying the breadth of meaning that TORAH and NOMOS do in the Bible. Infractions are SIN, with consequences in the life beyond as well as in this one. And the shariʿa does not simply REQUIRE, FORBID AND PERMIT — it also ADVISES, RECOMMENDS AND DISAPPROVES; it is thus MORE THAN LAW even in the broadest sense, setting before people ASPIRATIONS AS WELL AS DUTIES. As for sources: one may say there is ONLY ONE SOURCE AND THAT SOURCE IS GOD — which tells us that the law does NOT COME FROM HUMAN INSTITUTIONS, that APART FROM THE OBLIGATIONS GOD PLACES UPON US THERE ARE NO OBLIGATIONS AND APART FROM THE RIGHTS HE CONFERS THERE ARE NO RIGHTS, but LEAVES US IN THE DARK AS TO WHERE TO GO TO FIND GOD'S LAW. Hence the real question is not the source of the law but THE SOURCES OF KNOWLEDGE OF THE LAW.

cards.q: Why does Weiss distinguish the source of the law from the sources of KNOWLEDGE of the law?
cards.a: Because saying that God alone is the source explains the law's NATURE — it does not come from human institutions, and there are no obligations or rights but those God gives — while leaving us in the dark as to where to find it. The jurists' question is therefore epistemological: what are the sources of knowledge of God's law?
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: How does the shariʿa reach beyond law in the narrow sense?
cards.a: It embraces state law, ethical norms and ritual duties alike — carrying the breadth of torah and nomos — makes infractions SIN with consequences in the next life, and does not only require, forbid and permit but also ADVISES, RECOMMENDS AND DISAPPROVES, setting out aspirations as well as duties.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: The four sources — and why they are not four of the same thing
slides.text: The famous FOUR-SOURCE THEORY names the QURʾAN, the SUNNA, IJMĀʿ (consensus) and ANALOGICAL REASONING as USUL, literally 'ROOTS'. But they are not homogeneous. The QURʾAN AND THE SUNNA ARE MATERIAL SOURCES — they CONTAIN RULES WITHIN THEIR MEANING, to be extracted by interpretation. ANALOGICAL REASONING IS CLEARLY A METHOD, NOT A MATERIAL SOURCE, though a method that uses material sources to build law. IJMĀʿ is the hard case: the common view was that it TRANSFORMED OPINION INTO CERTAINTY, a tentative construction into a final one, once an opinion was shared by all living qualified scholars — the principle being 'MY COMMUNITY WILL NEVER CONCUR ON AN ERROR'. On that view the ijmāʿ BROUGHT ABOUT AN EPISTEMIC TRANSFORMATION WITHOUT ACTUALLY BECOMING A MATERIAL SOURCE, though some jurists held it could produce law on its own.

cards.q: Name the four sources of Islamic law and classify each.
cards.a: The Qurʾan and the Sunna — MATERIAL sources containing rules within their meaning. Analogical reasoning — a METHOD, not a material source, though one that works on material sources. Ijmāʿ, the consensus — on the common view neither, but an EPISTEMIC transformation turning opinion into certainty ('my community will never concur on an error'), though some jurists held it could produce law on its own.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Ijtihād: constructing a law that is not one's own
slides.text: The whole enterprise rests on the assumption that THE LAW OF GOD IS NOT GIVEN TO HUMANS AS A BODY OF READY-MADE NORMS: THE LAW IS FOR THE MOST PART SOMETHING THAT HUMANS CONSTRUCT ON THE BASIS OF REVEALED TEXTS — while never regarding it as of their own making. When jurists differed, as they generally did, this COULD ONLY MEAN THAT ALL BUT ONE — AND PERHAPS NOT EVEN WITH THE EXCEPTION OF ONE — WERE IN ERROR. The saving grace is the maxim 'DIFFERENCE OF OPINION IS A MERCY FROM GOD': as long as each scholar did his best and believed his construction true, EVEN IF HE HAD NOT ATTAINED FULL CERTAINTY, HIS CONSTRUCTION WAS CREDITED TO HIM AS VALID. The endeavour is IJTIHĀD ('effort'), its qualified practitioner a MUJTAHID ('one who toils'), and it presupposes a TEXT-CRITICAL PHASE — the methodologies of the science of hadith — before interpretation can begin. Once the variations crystallised into the MADHĀHIB, SCHOLARS TENDED TO BACK AWAY FROM THE RIGORS OF IJTIHĀD, resting in the confidence that the ijtihād embodied in the schools' traditions was sufficient for their times.

terms.def: The strenuous effort of constructing the law from the revealed texts, and the scholar qualified to undertake it.

cards.q: How can jurists disagree about a law that is God's alone, and what saves the disagreement?
cards.a: Because the law is not given ready-made: humans CONSTRUCT it from revealed texts, while never regarding it as their own making — so if jurists differ, all but one (perhaps all) are in error. The saving maxim is 'DIFFERENCE OF OPINION IS A MERCY FROM GOD': a scholar who did his best and believed his construction true had it credited as valid even without full certainty.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What happened to ijtihād once the schools of law had formed?
cards.a: Scholars tended to BACK AWAY from its rigours, resting in the confidence that the ijtihād which had gone into the doctrinal traditions of the schools was sufficient for their own times and an adequate basis for obedience to God's law.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: The genres, I: school texts, commentaries, glosses
slides.text: The MUTŪN (sing. MATN), 'SCHOOL TEXTS', embody the doctrine of a school and serve as its textbooks — but not every text of a school's doctrine is a matn: A MATN IS CHARACTERISED BY THE FACT THAT OTHER SCHOLARS OF THE SCHOOL HAVE RECOGNISED ITS DOCTRINAL IMPORTANCE AND COMMENTED UPON IT. Since the tenth century at the latest all schools have had their mutūn; STUDENTS LEARN THEM BY HEART, and only MINOR CHANGES have been introduced over the centuries, since they GUARANTEE THE CONTINUITY OF THE CORE OF A SCHOOL'S DOCTRINE. Movement happens elsewhere — in the COMMENTARIES (SHURŪḤ) and GLOSSES (ḤAWĀSHĪ), written in different regions and periods, which let us follow the geographical and historical recognition of a matn, record DISSENT WITHIN the school and the REPLACEMENT OF SOME OF ITS RULES BY NEWER ONES, refer to CHANGING SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS, and stress the difference between the CLASSICAL JURISTS (AL-MUTAQADDIMŪN) and the LATER JURISTS (AL-MUTAʾAKHKHIRŪN) — thereby underlining the DIACHRONIC character of the school doctrines. A fixed core with a moving commentary: that is how a law with no legislator changes.

terms.def: A 'school text': the memorised core of a school's doctrine, recognised as such by the school commenting on it, changed only minimally so as to preserve continuity.
The classical (early) jurists and the later ones — a distinction that becomes a major division of the law from the end of the 11th century, with priority given to the later.

cards.q: How does a law without a legislator change? Explain through the genres.
cards.a: The MUTŪN, the memorised school texts, stay almost unchanged, guaranteeing the continuity of the school's core doctrine. Change happens in the COMMENTARIES (shurūḥ) and GLOSSES (ḥawāshī), which record dissent within the school, the replacement of rules by newer ones, and changing social and economic conditions — and which distinguish the classical jurists from the later ones, making the doctrine's DIACHRONIC character explicit.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What makes a text a matn?
cards.a: Not its content alone but its RECEPTION: a matn is a text whose doctrinal importance the other scholars of the school have recognised BY COMMENTING UPON IT. Students then learn it by heart.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: The genres, II: the fatwa, ḥiyal, shurūṭ, rasāʾil
slides.text: The FATWA is the opinion of a MUFTI giving believers religious and legal guidance, and its peculiarity is that THE MUFTI CANNOT SIMPLY ENUMERATE OPINIONS OR FORMS OF DISSENT BUT MUST DECLARE ONE OPINION TO BE BINDING — 'the chosen opinion on which the fatwa is based' — and often the choice follows THE LATER ('MODERN') JURISTS while the classical opinions are EXPLICITLY DISCARDED. Two limits matter. A mufti asked by a qadi or the authorities DOES NOT CHECK THE FACTS — he decides what the doctrinal answer would be ASSUMING THE FACTS ARE TRUE, the examination of facts remaining the exclusive task of the qadi. And a mufti asked by an individual about an unintentional slip is NOT NECESSARILY OBLIGED to impose the school's norms: satisfied that the questioner will not repeat the misconduct, HE MAY EVEN ADVISE AGAINST TREATING IT AS A LEGAL PROBLEM — but SUCH RELIGIOUS GUIDANCE SHOULD ONLY BE GIVEN ORALLY, THE WRITTEN FORM REMAINING RESERVED TO JUDICIAL EXPERTISE. Hence the formula: THE FATWA REPRESENTS A LEVEL OF THE LAW IN WHICH LEGAL AND RELIGIOUS ASPECTS ARE DIFFERENTIATED BUT NOT SEPARATED. Beside it stand the books of LEGAL DEVICES (ḤIYAL) — Hanafi, from the eighth and ninth centuries — indicating THE LEGAL MEANS BY WHICH EXTRALEGAL PURPOSES MAY BE ACHIEVED, indispensable for understanding how the law was used to LEGALISE COMMERCIAL PRACTICES; the HANDBOOKS FOR NOTARIES (SHURŪṬ), a genre from the tenth century, entirely focused on the CORRECT WRITTEN FORM OF CONTRACTS and reflecting the merchants' interest in stable and credible legal forms; and the TREATISES (RASĀʾIL), in which prominent jurists defend CUSTOMS AND PRACTICES LINKED TO SPECIAL INTERESTS in critical political situations.

terms.def: A mufti's binding opinion for a questioner — he must choose ONE opinion, does not examine the facts (that is the qadi's task), and may give purely religious guidance orally only.
'Legal devices': the legal means by which extralegal purposes may be achieved — the Hanafi genre that shows how the law legalised commercial practice.

cards.q: What must a mufti do that a commentator need not, and what may he not do?
cards.a: He must DECLARE ONE OPINION BINDING rather than enumerate the dissent — often following the later jurists and explicitly discarding the classical ones. He may NOT examine the facts: he answers on the assumption that the facts as put are true, fact-finding being the qadi's exclusive task.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: Why may a mufti's advice to an individual be gentler than the school's norm — and why only orally?
cards.a: Because when asked for religious guidance about an unintentional slip, a mufti satisfied that the questioner will not repeat it may advise against treating it as a legal problem at all. That guidance must be ORAL: the written form is reserved to judicial expertise, so the indulgence never becomes a precedent. The fatwa is the level at which legal and religious aspects are differentiated but not separated.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What are ḥiyal and shurūṭ, and what do they reveal?
cards.a: Ḥiyal are books of 'legal devices' — the legal means by which EXTRALEGAL purposes may be achieved — first written by Hanafi jurists in the 8th and 9th centuries, indispensable for seeing how law legalised commercial practice; their status as part of the fiqh was disputed between schools. Shurūṭ are handbooks for notaries, a genre from the 10th century focused on the correct written form of contracts — evidence of the merchants' demand for stable, credible legal forms.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Qawāʿid and furūq: theory from below
slides.text: Beside the theologically inclined uṣūl al-fiqh there is a second theoretical approach, entirely dependent on the individual norms of a particular school. The QAWĀʿID, 'LEGAL PRINCIPLES', are found by ANALYSING GROUPS OF INDIVIDUAL NORMS AND DISCOVERING THE COMMON PRINCIPLES THAT UNITE THEM — and the principle then becomes AN INSTRUMENT THAT ALLOWS THE PRODUCTION OF NEW NORMS in line with the school's doctrine. Already Sarakhsi (d. 1090) credits Shaybani (d. 804) with linking disputed questions to their principles; it is in the FIFTEENTH CENTURY, according to Wolfhart Heinrichs, that jurists intensify 'the search for further general rules BY IMPLICIT INDUCTION from the great legal handbooks of the schools'. The FURŪQ literature of the Mamluk period does the converse: it COMPARES NORMS THAT SEEM TO BE BASED ON THE SAME PRINCIPLE BUT DO NOT PRODUCE THE SAME RULES, and explains the difference by finding a 'DETERMINING ELEMENT OF DIFFERENCE' that submits one of them to another principle. A famous sixteenth-century Egyptian author DECLARES THE THEORY OF COMMON LEGAL PRINCIPLES TO CONSTITUTE THE REAL THEORY OF THE LAW. Induction from the cases upward, against deduction from the revealed sources downward.

terms.def: Legal principles found by induction from groups of existing norms, and then used to produce new ones within a school's doctrine.
'Determining elements of difference': the Mamluk genre explaining why norms apparently resting on one principle yield different rules.

cards.q: Contrast qawāʿid and uṣūl al-fiqh as theories of law.
cards.a: Uṣūl al-fiqh reasons DOWNWARD from the revealed sources and carries a strong theological dimension. The qawāʿid work UPWARD: principles are found by induction from groups of existing norms of a particular school, and then serve to produce new norms in line with that doctrine — a theory entirely dependent on the positive law of the school. A 16th-century Egyptian author called the latter the real theory of the law.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What does the furūq literature do?
cards.a: It compares norms that appear to rest on the SAME principle yet produce DIFFERENT legal rules, and explains the divergence by finding a 'determining element of difference' that places one of them under another principle — resolving seemingly contradictory norm construction within the doctrine.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: The five qualifications, and the two forums
slides.text: The fiqh ranks ALL human acts in FIVE INTERCONNECTED CATEGORIES, agreed by all schools: OBLIGATORY (WĀJIB), RECOMMENDED (MANDŪB/SUNNA), INDIFFERENT OR PERMISSIBLE (MUBĀḤ), REPREHENSIBLE (MAKRŪH), FORBIDDEN (ḤARĀM). The Hanafis added a distinction between RELIGIOUS DUTY (FARḌ) and PURELY LEGAL OBLIGATION (WĀJIB): a legal obligation MUST BE FOLLOWED EVEN BY ONE WHO DOES NOT BELIEVE IN THE REASONING BEHIND IT, whereas a farḍ requires the subject BOTH TO ABIDE BY THE RULE AND TO BELIEVE IN ITS CHARACTER as a religious duty. INDIFFERENCE (IBĀḤA) WAS THE LAST CATEGORY TO BE ACCEPTED, still controversial in the eighth century — hard to reconcile with a sacred law determining the status of ALL acts, but it ALLOWED SCHOLARS TO TREAT CUSTOMARY SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC PRACTICES AS IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE SACRED LAW. The system separates law from ethics: A QADI IS NOT ENTITLED TO PROHIBIT ACTS OR IMPOSE OBLIGATIONS ON THE BASIS OF NORMS QUALIFYING ACTS AS INDIFFERENT, RECOMMENDABLE OR REPREHENSIBLE — those categories DIRECT THE CONSCIENCE; the qadi must decide on WĀJIB and ḤARĀM. Hence the compendia treat problems differently QAḌĀʾAN (judicially) and DIYĀNATAN (ethically), and hence the strongest expression of the distinction: the EXTERIOR FORUM (ẒĀHIR), the qadi's judgment, against the INTERIOR FORUM (BĀṬIN), 'BETWEEN THE BELIEVER AND HIS LORD'. A QADI'S JUDGMENT DOES NOT RENDER LICIT WHAT IS ILLICIT: a party who gained an unjustified advantage by a decision resting on false testimony SHOULD NOT USE IT.

terms.def: wājib (obligatory), mandūb (recommended), mubāḥ (indifferent), makrūh (reprehensible), ḥarām (forbidden). Only the first and last are enforceable by the qadi.
The exterior forum of the qadi's judgment and the interior forum 'between the believer and his Lord'. A judgment does not make the illicit licit.

cards.q: Name the five qualifications of human acts, and say which ones a qadi may act on.
cards.a: Obligatory (wājib), recommended (mandūb/sunna), indifferent (mubāḥ), reprehensible (makrūh), forbidden (ḥarām). The qadi may decide only on the MANDATORY and the FORBIDDEN: he may not prohibit or oblige on the basis of the indifferent, recommendable or reprehensible, which serve to direct the conscience of believers.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: Why was 'indifference' (ibāḥa) the last category to be accepted, and what did it make possible?
cards.a: Because a sacred law that determines the status of ALL human acts sits uneasily with a class of acts it does not evaluate. Its acceptance allowed the scholars to treat customary social and economic PRACTICES as being in accordance with the sacred law.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: Explain the interior and exterior forum with the standard example.
cards.a: The exterior forum (ẓāhir) is the qadi's judgment; the interior (bāṭin) is 'between the believer and his Lord'. A judgment does not render licit what is illicit: a woman irrevocably divorced by a triple declaration her husband denies, and which she cannot prove, remains legally married but knows before her own conscience that she is divorced and must refuse him. The party who gained an unjustified advantage by false testimony should not use it.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What is the Hanafi distinction between farḍ and wājib?
cards.a: A purely legal obligation (wājib) must be followed by everyone even by one who does not believe in the legal reasoning behind it; a religious duty (farḍ) requires the subject both to obey the rule AND to believe in its character as a religious duty. The other schools did not accept the distinction.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Property, religion, and the claims of God
slides.text: Contracts are VALID (ṢAḤĪḤ), NULL AND VOID (BĀṬIL) when a constituent element is missing, or VOIDABLE (FĀSID) when the elements exist but the object is insufficiently defined, the cause tainted by an inadmissible purpose, or the term uncertain. Religious affiliation then produces DEGREES OF PROPERTY. For NON-MUSLIMS, WINE AND SWINE ARE LEGALLY PROTECTED VALUABLE GOODS, since their own religious norms treat them so, and whoever destroys them OWES DAMAGES. For MUSLIMS the same things are LICIT PROPERTY THAT CAN NEITHER BE SOLD NOR BOUGHT, and their destruction GIVES NO CLAIM FOR DAMAGES — property whose content religion has voided while leaving the form in existence. A NON-MUSLIM MAY NOT USE THE SERVICES OF A MUSLIM SLAVE, because a Muslim must never be the slave of a non-Muslim, but NO ONE MAY SIMPLY DISREGARD HIS PROPERTY RIGHT: he is OBLIGED TO SELL and ENTITLED TO THE PRICE. Under a voidable sale the buyer acquires no right to use or consume — but IF HE SELLS ON TO A THIRD PERSON THE SALE IS VALID: THE ACT OF SELLING PURGES THE ILLICIT CHARACTER, so the first buyer is an owner FOR THE PURPOSES OF COMMERCIAL CIRCULATION AND NO FURTHER. Across all of this runs the classification of CLAIMS OF GOD (ḤUQŪQ ALLĀH) — the requirements protecting NOT PRIVATE CLAIMS BUT THE PUBLIC ORDER: worship, a number of penalties, and every norm serving 'the interest of all Muslims' — against CLAIMS OF MEN (ḤUQŪQ AL-NĀS), the subjective rights of human beings, Muslim or not. And the striking rule: CLAIMS OF GOD DO NOT NECESSARILY ENJOY PRECEDENCE, because HUMAN BEINGS DEPEND ON THEIR RIGHTS TO ESCAPE POVERTY AND NEED, WHILE GOD IS TOO EXALTED TO NEED THE FULFILMENT OF HIS CLAIMS — so where the two compete, priority is often given to THE CLAIM OF THE NEEDY PERSON OVER THE CLAIM OF GOD.

terms.def: Claims of God — norms protecting public order (worship, some penalties, the interest of all Muslims) — and claims of men, the subjective rights of persons. A universal classification across all fields of the law.
Valid; null and void (a constituent element missing); voidable (elements present but the object undefined, the cause tainted, or the term uncertain).

cards.q: Why may a claim of men take priority over a claim of God?
cards.a: Because human beings DEPEND on the fulfilment of their rights to escape poverty and need, while God is 'too exalted and sublime to need the fulfilment of his claims'. Where the two compete the jurists often prefer the claim of the needy person — and Muslims are told not to testify against fellow Muslims in trials over God's claims, out of the 'recommended covering up' of others' faults.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: How does religion produce degrees of property in the fiqh? Give the wine-and-swine case.
cards.a: For non-Muslims wine and swine are legally protected valuable goods — destroying them obliges the destroyer to pay damages. For Muslims they are licit PROPERTY that may neither be used, sold nor bought, and whose destruction gives NO claim for damages: the religious prohibition empties the property right of content while leaving it formally in existence.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: How can selling on illicitly acquired property make it licit?
cards.a: Under a voidable contract of sale the buyer acquires no right to use or consume the object; but if he sells it on to a third person, THAT sale is valid. The reintroduction into commercial circulation PURGES the illicit character and gives the first buyer a valid title — but only as far as circulation requires: he still may not keep, use or consume it.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Punishment: ḥudūd, talio, and the principle of doubt
slides.text: Within transactions the ḤUDŪD — fixed punishments imposed as CLAIMS OF GOD: capital punishment for robbery and illicit sexual relations, amputation for theft, lashes for wine drinking and false accusation — are marked off from everything else by PROCEDURE AND PROOF, as is QIṢĀṢ (talio) for intentional homicide, which is conceived as A RIGHT OF THE VICTIM'S FAMILY: they may DEMAND ITS EXECUTION, ARRANGE A SETTLEMENT, OR RENOUNCE ANY CLAIM — a three-way choice showing it to be their PRIVATE right. Neither may be imposed where a relevant SHUBHA exists, and the maxim runs: 'THE FIXED PUNISHMENTS OF THE LAW BECOME INAPPLICABLE IF DOUBTS EXIST' (AL-ḤUDŪD TUDRAʾU BI-L-SHUBUHĀT). Doubt has THREE DIMENSIONS: SUBJECTIVE ERROR of the perpetrator (he believed himself entitled); OBJECTIVE DOUBT (he mistook another woman for his wife, or killed a man he took for a beast); and PROCEDURAL DOUBT arising from INDIRECT EVIDENCE such as hearsay. Further peculiarities: WOMEN ARE NOT ACCEPTED AS WITNESSES in these trials; if witnesses WITHDRAW their testimony AFTER the condemnation the accused IS RELEASED, by JURISTIC PREFERENCE (ISTIḤSĀN) and CONTRARY TO ANALOGY, which would leave the judgment standing; an avowal may be revoked; and possible witnesses are admonished to 'VEIL' THE SLIPS OF THEIR FELLOW MUSLIMS. But the special status does NOT extend to all corporal punishment: TAʿZĪR, 'chastisement', has NO DEFINED CRIME, NO PRESCRIBED PROCEDURE AND NO FIXED PENALTY — in the classical period kept below the least hadd penalty, but GROWING RAPIDLY IN IMPORTANCE afterwards, so that in the NINETEENTH CENTURY capital punishment was imposed for behaviour the classical fiqh had never punished so harshly. So the protective doubt principle guards precisely the punishments BASED ON REVEALED TEXTS — and the discretionary track beside them was the one that expanded.

terms.def: Doubt excluding a hadd or talio punishment, in three forms: the perpetrator's subjective error, objective error about the object, and procedural doubt from indirect evidence.
Discretionary chastisement: no defined crime, no prescribed procedure, no fixed penalty — and therefore none of the protections of the doubt principle.

cards.q: State the doubt maxim and its three forms.
cards.a: 'The fixed punishments of the law become inapplicable if doubts exist' (al-ḥudūd tudraʾu bi-l-shubuhāt). The three forms: SUBJECTIVE error of the perpetrator (he thought himself entitled); OBJECTIVE doubt (he mistook another woman for his wife, or a man for a beast); and PROCEDURAL doubt from indirect evidence such as hearsay.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: Why is qiṣāṣ (talio) called a private right?
cards.a: Because the competent members of the victim's family have a three-way choice: demand its execution from the judiciary, arrange a settlement with the perpetrator, or renounce any claim at all. The state does not prosecute intentional homicide on its own account.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What is taʿzīr, and why does it matter for judging the 'penal law of Islam'?
cards.a: Discretionary chastisement with no defined crime, no prescribed procedure and no fixed penalty — and therefore outside the protective doubt principle, which guards only the punishments grounded in revealed texts. In the classical period it stayed below the lowest hadd penalty, but it grew rapidly afterwards, and by the nineteenth century capital punishment was imposed under it for behaviour the classical fiqh had never punished so harshly.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: How does religious affiliation affect punishment and tort?
cards.a: Non-Muslims are not stoned for illicit sexual relations and are not punished at all for drinking wine. Most Sunni schools assign unequal blood money to Muslim and non-Muslim lives and do not impose capital punishment on a Muslim for killing a non-Muslim; only the HANAFIS hold blood money equal and execute Muslims and non-Muslims alike for homicide against either. All schools agree that non-Muslims may not testify against Muslims.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Spheres of the law: against Schacht
slides.text: Joseph Schacht held that 'NONE OF THE MODERN SYSTEMATIC DISTINCTIONS, BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC LAW, OR BETWEEN CIVIL AND PENAL LAW, OR BETWEEN SUBSTANTIVE AND ADJECTIVE LAW, EXISTS WITHIN THE RELIGIOUS LAW OF ISLAM… THE CONCEPT OF ANY SYSTEMATIC DISTINCTION IS LACKING', and arranged his own exposition according to the divisions of MODERN legal science instead. Johansen's answer: the jurists DID differentiate spheres, only not by abstract concepts — they used THE INTENT OF THE ACTORS, THE LAW OF PROCEDURE AND PROOF, CONTRACT TERMINOLOGY AND THE PURPOSE OF THE ACTS. WORSHIP: all acts require a DECLARATION OF INTENT (NIYYA) — the only sphere where all acts do; they are owed ONLY BY MUSLIMS, since non-Muslims lack the capacity to perform them; mistakes are SINS, NOT CRIMES, and the qadi does not correct prayers — a Muslim accused of neglecting them is BELIEVED ON HIS WORD, as one in a fiduciary relationship with God (AMĪN); yet one who admits persistent neglect without excuse faces, in three of the four Sunni schools, CAPITAL PUNISHMENT (the Hanafis are content with imprisonment). COMMERCE: defined by PROFIT — Jassas: 'COMMERCIAL EXCHANGE IS A NAME APPLIED TO BILATERAL RECIPROCAL CONTRACTS THE PURPOSE OF WHICH IS THE QUEST FOR PROFIT'; Sarakhsi: 'THE SALE HAS NOT BEEN INSTITUTED EXCEPT FOR THE SEARCH OF PROFIT AND SURPLUS' — and hence the requirement that genus, kind, quality and quantity be exactly declared, since the contract is a means of INFORMATION about exchange value. Commercial contracts are built on CALCULATION, HARASSMENT (MUḌĀYAQA) AND HAGGLING (MUMĀKASA); marriage, consensual divorce and settlement on INDULGENCE AND GENEROSITY, since — as Kasani puts it — A HUMAN BEING NORMALLY TOLERATES FOR HIS PERSON WHAT HE DOES NOT TOLERATE FOR HIS PROPERTY. MARRIAGE AND FAMILY: distinguished by STRICT FORMALISM — any declaration expressing the will to marry, to emancipate a slave, or to repudiate is BINDING ON ITS AUTHOR WITH NO INTENT REQUIRED — while the financial consideration is treated loosely, because IT IS THE SOCIAL STATUS AND NOT THE FINANCIAL CONSIDERATION THAT MATTERS. Sarakhsi's principle of interpretation covers the whole: 'IT IS THE PURPOSE THAT IS RELEVANT. CONTRACTS DIFFER THROUGH PURPOSE, NOT THROUGH THE CONSIDERATION OF THEIR EXPRESSIONS.'

cards.q: What is Schacht's thesis about the structure of Islamic law, and how does Johansen answer it?
cards.a: Schacht: none of the modern systematic distinctions — public/private, civil/penal, substantive/adjective — exists in Islamic law, and 'the concept of any systematic distinction is lacking'. Johansen answers that the jurists DID differentiate spheres, only not through abstract concepts: they used the actors' INTENT, the law of PROCEDURE AND PROOF, contract terminology and the PURPOSE of the acts. Schacht measured one legal system by the categories of another and recorded the gaps.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: How is the sphere of worship marked off from all other spheres?
cards.a: All its acts require a declaration of INTENT (niyya) — the only sphere in which that is so; its obligations are owed by MUSLIMS ONLY, non-Muslims being incapable of performing them; mistakes are sins, not crimes, and the qadi does not correct them — the accused is believed on his word as one trusted (amīn) before God. Yet persistent admitted neglect brings capital punishment in three of the four Sunni schools, imprisonment among the Hanafis.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: Contrast the commercial sphere with marriage and family in the fiqh.
cards.a: Commerce is defined by PROFIT — 'the sale has not been instituted except for the search of profit and surplus' — hence the exact declaration of genus, quality and quantity, and contracts built on calculation, harassment and haggling. Marriage, consensual divorce and settlement rest on INDULGENCE AND GENEROSITY, since a person tolerates for his PERSON what he will not tolerate for his PROPERTY; they are strictly formal — any clear declaration binds without intent — but loose about the financial consideration, because the social STATUS is the point.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: Quote Sarakhsi's principle of contract interpretation.
cards.a: 'It is the PURPOSE that is relevant. Contracts differ through purpose, not through the consideration of their expressions.' Hence a clear choice of contract type itself expresses intent.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: Motzki: the Sunna and the problem of authenticity
slides.text: Two sources are singled out as the divine basis: the QURʾAN — God's word, literally reproduced, accurately transmitted, finally written down — and the SUNNA, meaning LEGALLY RELEVANT WORDS OR ACTIONS OF THE PROPHET OR HIS TACIT CONSENT to current practices. Its authority rests on Qurʾanic verses calling believers to obey the Prophet, and on the Sunna itself. The rank is explained precisely: the Sunna too is of divine origin, since the Prophet is assumed to have been divinely inspired, BUT THE TEXTS IN WHICH IT IS ARTICULATED ARE HUMAN SPEECH — his own or his companions' — SO ONLY THE CONTENT, NOT THE WORDING, IS OF DIVINE ORIGIN, which gives it SECOND rank. What is debated is whether the Sunna is INDEPENDENT of the Qurʾan and whether either can ABROGATE the other; the majority allow abrogation on conditions. Authenticity is the hard problem: NEITHER SOURCE EXISTS AS AN AUTOGRAPH. For the Qurʾan the scholars answer that SO MANY PEOPLE OF EACH GENERATION TRANSMITTED IT that loss or distortion is improbable. For the Sunna, a hadith is authentic if its transmission is UNBROKEN (MUTTAṢIL) — no gaps in the chain of transmitters, the ISNĀD — and RECURRENT (MUTAWĀTIR) — many transmitters in each generation, especially the first three, spreading it INDEPENDENTLY of each other, the number large enough to PRECLUDE COLLUSION (five, twelve, twenty, seventy are proposed; the more the better). Such a hadith gives the same sure knowledge as a Qurʾanic verse and may even abrogate one. But the theorists know that FEW traditions meet the test: most are ḤADĪTH AL-ĀḤĀD, SOLITARY REPORTS, giving only PROBABILITY — and the majority hold these CAN AND MUST BE USED FOR LEGAL RULES IN RELIGIOUS PRACTICE BUT NOT IN MATTERS OF BELIEF. Since their weight then depends on the individual transmitter, the chains must be studied and the transmitters graded — TRUSTWORTHY (THIQA), RELIABLE (THABT), SINCERE (ṢADŪQ), WEAK (ḌAʿĪF), MENDACIOUS (KADHDHĀB) — and the hadiths in turn SOUND (ṢAḤĪḤ), SATISFACTORY (ḤASAN) or WEAK (ḌAʿĪF).

terms.def: The chain of transmitters accompanying a hadith; its unbrokenness is one of the two conditions of authenticity.
Recurrent transmission by many independent transmitters in each generation, yielding certainty — against the solitary report of one or few, yielding only probability.

cards.q: Why does the Sunna rank second to the Qurʾan even though both are divine?
cards.a: Because the Prophet is assumed to have been divinely INSPIRED in his legally relevant words and acts, but the texts articulating the Sunna are HUMAN SPEECH — his own or his companions' — so only the CONTENT, not the wording, is of divine origin. The Qurʾan is God's own speech.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What two conditions make a hadith authentic, and what follows if they are met?
cards.a: The transmission must be UNBROKEN (muttaṣil) — no gaps in the isnād — and RECURRENT (mutawātir) — many transmitters in each generation, especially the first three, transmitting independently, in numbers large enough to preclude collusion. Such a hadith yields the same sure knowledge as a Qurʾanic verse and may specify or even abrogate one, provided it is unambiguous.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What is a solitary hadith, and how may it be used?
cards.a: Ḥadīth al-āḥād: one transmitted by only one or a few transmitters in the first three generations — the normal case. It yields not certainty but a reasonable supposition, and the majority of legal scholars hold it can and must be used to back legal rules IN RELIGIOUS PRACTICE BUT NOT IN MATTERS OF BELIEF. Its weight then depends on the quality of the individual transmitters, who are graded from trustworthy (thiqa) to mendacious (kadhdhāb).
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

slides.title: The Western debate, and what it is not about
slides.text: Many Western specialists doubt the authenticity of the legal hadiths — and the article is careful about what that means: THEY DO NOT INTEND TO UNDERMINE THE IDEA THAT THE SUNNA IS A DIVINE SOURCE OF LAW; IN THEIR VIEW THIS IS A QUESTION OF NORMS AND BELIEF, NOT OF FACTS AND EMPIRIC SCHOLARSHIP. They ask instead which hadiths can serve as sources for reconstructing which period. Two arguments are made. First, an origin in the Prophet's time is improbable because THE HADITHS OF THE PROPHET SEEM TO BE A LATE ELEMENT IN THE DISCUSSIONS OF EIGHTH-CENTURY JURISTS: HAD THEY EXISTED FROM THE BEGINNING THEY WOULD HAVE BEEN USED AS LEGAL ARGUMENTS, AND THERE WOULD HAVE BEEN NO DEBATE ABOUT THEIR RANK AS A LEGAL SOURCE. Second, the very pattern of solitary transmission followed by wide diffusion in the eighth century is held to be AN ANOMALY THAT CANNOT REFLECT REAL TRANSMISSION but points to fabrication of the isnād by the supposed transmitter of the third generation — the 'COMMON LINK'. Against this, other scholars study THE TRANSMISSION HISTORY OF INDIVIDUAL HADITHS, dating them by comparing isnāds, textual variants, the sources in which they appear and the data on the transmitters; in their view THE COMMON LINK CAN ALSO BE A TRANSMITTING COLLECTOR, NOT NECESSARILY A FABRICATOR. By that route several hadiths have been traced back to the first Islamic century — and one of the few assumed to be recurrent turned out to be only 'well known' (MASHHŪR), going back to a single companion and not transmitted literally. The honest conclusion: AN EARLY DATE DOES NOT MEAN THE HADITH ACTUALLY REPORTS A SAYING OR ACTION OF THE PROPHET — THIS REMAINS AN OPEN QUESTION THAT SO FAR CANNOT BE ANSWERED BY WESTERN SCHOLARLY METHODS.

terms.def: The transmitter at the point where a solitary chain branches into many. Read by some as the fabricator of the isnād, by others as simply a transmitting collector.

cards.q: What is the 'common link', and why do scholars read it in opposite ways?
cards.a: The transmitter — usually of the third generation — at whom a solitary transmission chain suddenly branches into many. Sceptics treat that pattern as an anomaly that cannot reflect real transmission, and so as evidence that he FABRICATED the isnād; others hold he may simply have been a transmitting COLLECTOR, and by dating individual hadiths have traced several back to the first Islamic century.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: What is the Western scepticism about hadiths NOT claiming, and where does the question end?
cards.a: It is not claiming that the Sunna is not a divine source of law — that is a question of norms and belief, not of empirical scholarship. The question is which hadiths can be used to reconstruct which period. And even an early date does not show that a hadith reports a saying or action of the Prophet himself: that remains open and, so far, unanswerable by Western methods.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law

cards.q: Give the argument from silence against an early origin of the legal hadiths.
cards.a: That the hadiths of the Prophet appear as a LATE element in the discussions of eighth-century jurists: had they existed from the seventh century they would have been used as legal arguments at once, and there would have been no debate about their rank as a source of law.
cards.topic: Ancient Legal Cultures; History of Islamic Law
